# As drone delivery scales up, retailers run into range limits and noise complaints

Article by Zak Stambor | Nov 13, 2026

The news: Drone delivery is rapidly moving from small-scale tests to broader rollouts.

- Drone delivery startup Zipline, which earlier this month raised $1.5 billion at a $21.5 billion valuation, is seeing a surge in retailer interest. Just months ago, the company was targeting the capacity to make 1 million deliveries a day. Now, three or four retailers are each interested in purchasing that volume, per The Wall Street Journal.
- Walmart has completed more than 2 million drone deliveries, double the number it reported in May. The retailer also announced plans to add 300 sites through an expanded agreement with Zipline, bringing its planned network to at least 570 sites, nearly nine times the 66 it operated at the start of the year.
- Amazon plans to expand Prime Air drone delivery to nearly 500 US cities and towns by the end of the year, six times its previous footprint. The company announced the expansion in August and recently launched service in markets including suburban Chicago.
- DoorDash is testing drone delivery beyond restaurants, partnering with Lowe’s in North Carolina alongside restaurant pilots with Chipotle and Popeyes in Northern California.

Why this matters: Expanding service puts drones within reach of more customers, but it also exposes retailers to a new set of operational and consumer acceptance hurdles.

Limited range and capacity: Drones promise faster, more efficient deliveries to remote locations, but their limited range constrains that potential for now. Wing’s drones have a round-trip range of up to 12 miles, while Amazon Prime Air’s can travel about 7 miles. Weight limits narrow their usefulness further. Amazon’s drones can carry packages that weigh 5 pounds or less and fit inside a large shoebox, while Walmart’s limits range from 2 to 8 pounds, depending on the provider.

Noise complaints: Within two weeks of Amazon launching drone delivery in Nampa, Idaho, officials in Nampa and neighboring Meridian told KTVB that they had received multiple complaints about noise and frequent flights. Amazon then began evaluating changes, including adjustments to flight paths.

Botched deliveries: In August, a video of an Amazon drone dropping a customer's order of cat food and shoe insoles into water went viral, drawing nationwide media attention that highlighted the risks of deliveries gone wrong.

Implications for retailers: Drones are one piece of a much broader push to shrink delivery windows. Speed is already a deciding factor for shoppers: 23% say delivery speed is the most important aspect of the online delivery experience, and nearly two-thirds are willing to pay $7 to $9 for ultrafast delivery, per a January Metapack and Retail Economics report. The payoff goes beyond a single sale: Doug Herrington, CEO of Worldwide Amazon Stores, has said faster delivery makes shoppers more likely to buy, return sooner, and spend more.

Amazon is building speed into its entire network, with plans to grow its same-day fulfillment network from about 85 facilities to more than 1,000 by 2031, putting one within 10 miles of 80% of US Prime members, per Business Insider. Walmart can already deliver to 95% of US households in under 3 hours, and use of its Express Delivery service rose 48% YoY in Q2.

These investments also reinforce Amazon’s competitive advantage. Selling access to its logistics network through Amazon Supply Chain Services (ASCS), launched in May, creates a new revenue stream that Amazon can reinvest in scale and efficiency, making it harder for competitors to keep up.

Given their current range and weight limits, drones complement ground delivery for convenience items rather than replace it. Retailers expanding drone service should also engage local officials and residents early to address concerns before they escalate, as Amazon's experience with noise complaints in Nampa illustrates.
